extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and practitioners of digital media, viral_marketing, and meme studies
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the features that make online content spread (virality) and/or generate user-created derivatives (memetic success), including classification of meme types and practical drivers of sharing and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic dimensions (content, form, stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared features that define a meme may include content (ideas), form (format), and stance; the definition of a meme’s scope may rely on the dimension through which it is examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prism is content, the same content can appear as video, text, or image and be considered the same meme across forms; if the prism is format, memetic formats (e.g., image macros, lip-synch) group items that convey many ideas. Choose the dimension (content, form, or stance) to set the boundaries of what counts as one meme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality — three key attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Virality is a cascade diffusion process characterized by (1) a person-to-person mode of diffusion; (2) great speed, enhanced by social media; and (3) broad reach across multiple networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate viral items by checking whether they spread via active forwarding across weakly linked personal networks, how rapidly exposures increased, and whether they bridged multiple networks to achieve broad reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viral vs. memetic distinction (variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A viral is a single cultural unit (video, photo, joke) that propagates in many copies; an Internet meme is always a collection of texts/versions—variability is the defining difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label a single video as 'viral' but only call it memetic when significant derivatives emerge. Example: Chris Crocker’s 'Leave Britney Alone' was a viral that became memetic only after many derivatives appeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of diffusion: viral, founder-based meme, egalitarian meme
rubrics_metrics.description: Threefold differentiation: (1) Viral — one item spreading to millions; (2) Founder-based meme — sparked by a specific (often viral) founding text followed by many lesser-viewed versions; (3) Egalitarian meme — many versions evolving simultaneously without a clear founding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table attributes to classify: number of versions, distribution of popularity (winner-take-most vs even), viewer counts of initial item, focus of derivatives (people relate to a specific clip vs a formula), user involvement, and whether derivatives modify text. Examples: Evian Roller Babies (viral), 'Pepper-Spraying Cop' (founder-based), LOLCats (egalitarian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame of analysis: transmission vs ritual (modes of engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes and virals can be analyzed either as transmission (movement of items across space/networks) or as ritual (construction of shared beliefs and identities); these framings yield different evaluative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transmission framing asks about diffusion patterns and success factors (who spreads it, how far, speed); a ritual framing asks about cultural implications, identity formation, and what shared values the content constructs. Consider both perspectives to get a fuller assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (and humor) — a driver of sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: People are more likely to share positive than negative stories; they also prefer surprising, interesting, or practically useful items. Humor is central to virality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether content elicits positive valence and surprise. Humor often increases shareability because it makes senders appear entertaining and elicits pleasurable responses in recipients. Viral-content designers should favor upbeat, surprising material when targeting broad sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provoking high-arousal emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that provokes high-arousal emotions (positive or negative) spreads more: 'Awa/Wow' positive high-arousal and negative high-arousal (anger/anxiety) both encourage sharing; plain sadness (low-arousal) does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emotional arousal level: does the piece generate elevation/wonder or anger/anxiety that activates recipients to act (e.g., share, comment)? Use examples like Kony 2012 (anger/anxiety) and awe-inspiring stories for illustration. Avoid relying solely on low-arousal sadness for virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging (simplicity and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, simple messages and easy-to-decode formats spread better than complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check if the message defines the problem and solution plainly and is easy to understand quickly (Kony 2012’s simple problem/solution framing is a cited example). Simplicity aids shareability but can also oversimplify complex issues (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige (source fame and endorsements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame or recognizable sources increase spread: people are likelier to share content authored or endorsed by high-prestige figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider author/source reputation and celebrity seeding strategies (e.g., recruiting celebrities to amplify a campaign). 'Attention philanthropy'—mobilizing celebrities—can boost diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning (placement and seeding strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where content is placed (editorial prominence, platform location) and to whom it is seeded (hubs and bridges) critically affect viral diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial prominence (homepage placement, featured slots) and seeding to high-centrality users: 'hubs' with many connections and 'bridges' connecting otherwise separate communities. Also account for organized clusters of committed actors who can trigger spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation (encouraging additional actions and re-creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virality is enhanced when audiences are invited not only to share but to take further actions—sign petitions, send premade tweets—or to re-create/appropriate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess campaign affordances for user engagement beyond forwarding: does it provide premade messages, calls to action, or templates for personalizing content? Participation deepens involvement and can convert sharing into political/commercial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic-video feature: ordinary people (user-generated content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic videos often focus on ordinary people (user-generated) rather than celebrities, making them easier to imitate and more appealing for peer-to-peer response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check origin (user-generated vs professional) and protagonists; user-generated clips tend to generate more video responses and text discussion. Ordinary-person protagonists set achievable imitation goals and invite community interaction (peers can reply and validate imitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic-video feature: flawed masculinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many memetic videos feature male protagonists who fail to meet conventional masculinity norms (appearance or behavior), a recurrent representational pattern in the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note gendered patterns: flawed or non-hegemonic masculine portrayals (e.g., awkwardness, effeminacy, physical atypicality) appear frequently and can be framed comically; assess whether imitators mock or venerate such protagonists as part of interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic-video feature: humor (playfulness, incongruity, superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a major component of memetic videos and operates through playfulness, incongruity (especially audio-visual mismatch), and superiority dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humor: (a) playfulness invites participation via a game-like frame; (b) incongruity—unexpected juxtapositions or audio/visual mismatch—creates puzzles users may remix; (c) superiority (laughing at perceived inferiority) motivates mocking imitations. Identify which comic attribute is operative and how it drives derivative creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic-video feature: simplicity (idea and production)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic videos commonly convey a single uncomplicated idea, often with one or two performers, simple frames/settings, and frequently one-shot/unedited production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess conceptual simplicity (one clear idea or slogan) and production simplicity (single take, plain background, domestic setting). Simplicity facilitates imitation and lowers barriers for derivative creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic-video feature: repetitiveness and whimsical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitiveness (catchy phrases or repeated moves) and whimsical, playful content are common in memetic videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for refrains, repeated hooks, or whimsical motifs that make replication easy (e.g., dance moves, recurring catchphrases). These patterns become templates users can reuse and adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification criterion: high derivative volume
rubrics_metrics.description: A working definition of a 'memetic video' is an exceptionally popular video that generates a high volume of derivatives (remakes, parodies, responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use platform metrics (most viewed/responded/discussed/favorited) and manual screening for derivative counts (as done in the cited study) to identify memetic items. High view counts alone are insufficient; derivative production is the key marker.
